text: Lesson 13's UI Test simulated a user clicking through an actual form. A server-side Test skips all of that. Instead of interacting with the interface, its Test Steps call into server-side logic directly — running a method on a Script Include, or creating and modifying a record — with no form rendering and no page to wait on.

Course 6 built reusable, class-based Script Includes as the single source of truth for a piece of logic. A server-side Test Step can call one of those methods directly, pass it a known input, and assert the return value matches what's expected — catching a broken contract immediately, without reconstructing the form interaction that would eventually surface the same bug.

The other common server-side step works through GlideRecord directly: create or modify a record under known conditions, the same way a Business Rule would encounter it, and check the resulting record's state. This confirms a before-insert Business Rule actually aborted an insert, or that a field ended up with the correct value, with nothing about the UI involved.

A UI Test and a server-side Test are not two ways of testing the same thing. A UI Test confirms the end-user experience works. A server-side Test confirms the underlying logic works, independent of whatever form eventually calls it.

A Script Include's logic can be completely correct while a UI Policy on the form that calls it is broken — a server-side Test would pass while only a UI Test catches that. Just as easily, a form can look and behave perfectly while the logic behind it silently returns the wrong answer.
Real ATF coverage for anything non-trivial uses both layers, each catching what the other structurally cannot. Next up: grouping individual Tests into Test Suites and running them on a schedule.
